hints: Start by thinking about where antibodies naturally come from in a mammal and why you need to first trigger that process on purpose.
Recall which organ is rich in activated B-lymphocytes and what two cell properties you need to combine - making the right antibody and dividing forever.
Think about what type of cancer cell divides indefinitely but does not make the wanted antibody, and how you could join it to an antibody-making cell.
Consider why not every fused cell will be useful and so what testing step must follow fusion before large-scale production.
Remember the meaning of mono- in monoclonal and what you must do with the single correct cell to get large identical amounts.
walkthrough:
Trigger the Right Immune Response**
You need B-cells that already make antibody against your target. Injecting a foreign specific antigen into a mouse starts a normal humoral response. Over several weeks, B-lymphocytes are activated, divide and become plasma cells secreting that antibody.

Collect the Antibody Factories**
Those activated B-lymphocytes collect in the spleen. Removing splenocytes gives you cells that make the desired antibody, but on their own they die quickly in culture and cannot be grown long-term.

Create Immortal Hybridomas**
Fuse the splenocytes with myeloma cells, which are cancer cells that divide indefinitely. Fusion, using e.g. polyethylene glycol as fusogen, creates hybridoma cells that have both properties - they secrete the specific antibody and they divide continuously.

Select and Clone the Winner**
Many fusion products form, so you screen using HAT medium and test for binding to the antigen to select only the hybridoma making the wanted antibody. Then you clone that single cell by growing it in separate wells, so all daughter cells produce identical monoclonal antibodies in large amounts.

Final answer: Inject specific foreign antigen into a small mammal, e.g. mouse, and leave time for immune response. Remove B-lymphocytes/splenocytes from spleen. Fuse splenocytes with myeloma/tumour cells to form hybridomas. Screen and select correct hybridoma cells, then clone selected cells to produce monoclonal antibodies.

hints: Look at the Y-shaped molecule in Fig. 6.1 and recall which end of a normal antibody binds antigen and which end is constant.
Find the small shapes on the surface of the platelets that match the shape of the tips of the Y - these must fit together like lock and key.
Distinguish the stem of the Y from its two forked tips to separate constant region from binding site.
walkthrough:
Read the Antibody Shape**
Abciximab is drawn as a Y. The two tips of the fork are the variable regions that form the antigen binding sites. The single stem is the constant region, identical in many antibodies.

Match Labels Q and R**
In Fig. 6.1, Q points to the stem of the Y, so Q is the constant region. R points to one tip of the fork, so R is one of the antigen binding sites.

Find the Target on the Platelet**
The binding sites must attach to a complementary molecule on the platelet surface. S points to that small surface receptor/antigen on the platelet, while T points to the platelet itself. That surface molecule is the target antigen blocked by abciximab, preventing platelets binding together.
Final answer: target antigen for abciximab: S (accept T); constant region of abciximab: Q; one antigen binding site of abciximab: R.

hints: Recall where the pacemaker that starts each heartbeat sits - think which chamber receives blood from the vena cava.
Trace the impulse from AV node toward the apex and recall the name of the special fast-conducting muscle fibres in the ventricle walls.
Link ventricular muscle contraction to pressure change and recall the term systole versus diastole.
walkthrough:
Where the Wave Starts**
The sinoatrial node is the pacemaker. It sits in the wall of the right atrium near where the vena cava enters. Impulses spread across the atria causing atrial systole, then reach the atrioventricular node.

Fast Route to the Apex**
From the AV node there is a short delay, then impulses travel rapidly down the Bundle of His and Purkyne tissue / fibres toward the apex. This special muscle conducts quickly so the ventricles contract from the bottom up.

Pressure Up When Ventricles Squeeze**
When ventricular muscle contracts, ventricular volume falls and pressure rises sharply, forcing semilunar valves open. Contraction of a chamber is systole, so this stage is ventricular systole.
Final answer: right atrium; Purkyne tissue / fibres (accept Bundle of His); ventricular systole.
